lesson.title: The SDN Controller: One Brain, Many Switches
lesson.summary: The SDN controller is the centralized software that maintains a network wide view of topology and state, and uses OpenFlow to translate high level intent into the flow rules installed on every switch.
lesson.body:
OpenFlow gives a controller a way to talk to switches, install flow entries, and receive packets the switches do not know how to handle. But a protocol alone does not decide anything, it just carries messages. The SDN controller is the software that actually makes the decisions, the piece that used to be scattered across every individual router's control plane and is now centralized into one program, or a small cluster of cooperating programs, with a view of the network as a whole rather than just one device's local neighborhood.

A controller typically does three things. First, it discovers and maintains a model of the network's topology: which switches exist, how they are connected, what hosts are attached where, often by having switches report link status and by sending small discovery packets across the network. Second, it exposes what is usually called a northbound interface, an API that applications and operators can use to express intent, such as keep traffic under 70 percent of link capacity, or isolate this group of hosts from that one, without writing raw flow table entries by hand. Third, it translates that intent, combined with its topology view, into the actual OpenFlow messages, flow-mod calls that install, update, or remove entries, that get pushed down to the switches that need them.

Consider a data center fabric with dozens of switches, where a link between two switches starts approaching saturation. A switch making decisions purely on local information has no way to know that an alternate path exists three hops away with spare capacity, it can only work with what it can see. A controller with a full topology view can recognize the congestion, recompute better paths for the flows crossing that link, and push updated flow entries to every switch along the new path in a coordinated way. That kind of network wide traffic engineering is difficult to achieve when every device is making independent, locally scoped decisions, and much more natural when one system can see the whole picture.

This centralization is also the controller's biggest liability. If the controller goes down or becomes unreachable, switches can typically keep forwarding traffic using whatever rules are already installed, but they generally cannot adapt to new conditions, install new flows for traffic they have not seen before, or respond to failures, until control is restored. Real deployments address this with clustering and redundancy rather than relying on a single controller instance, but the underlying tradeoff, a single logical brain gives you coordinated, network wide intelligence at the cost of a critical dependency, is inherent to the SDN model. Open source projects such as ONOS and OpenDaylight are examples of SDN controller platforms built around this design.
